Mathers Foundation","id":[{"id":"https:\/\/ror.org\/02a7hjv13","id-type":"ROR","asserted-by":"crossref"}]}],"content-domain":{"domain":[],"crossmark-restriction":false},"short-container-title":["Hippocampus"],"published-print":{"date-parts":[[2015,10]]},"abstract":"<jats:title>ABSTRACT<\/jats:title>\n                  <jats:p>Sharp wave ripples (SPW\u2010Rs) represent the most synchronous population pattern in the mammalian brain. Their excitatory output affects a wide area of the cortex and several subcortical nuclei. SPW\u2010Rs occur during \u201coff\u2010line\u201d states of the brain, associated with consummatory behaviors and non\u2010REM sleep, and are influenced by numerous neurotransmitters and neuromodulators. They arise from the excitatory recurrent system of the CA3 region and the SPW\u2010induced excitation brings about a fast network oscillation (ripple) in CA1. The spike content of SPW\u2010Rs is temporally and spatially coordinated by a consortium of interneurons to replay fragments of waking neuronal sequences in a compressed format. SPW\u2010Rs assist in transferring this compressed hippocampal representation to distributed circuits to support memory consolidation; selective disruption of SPW\u2010Rs interferes with memory. Recently acquired and pre\u2010existing information are combined during SPW\u2010R replay to influence decisions, plan actions and, potentially, allow for creative thoughts. In addition to the widely studied contribution to memory, SPW\u2010Rs may also affect endocrine function via activation of hypothalamic circuits. Alteration of the physiological mechanisms supporting SPW\u2010Rs leads to their pathological conversion, \u201cp\u2010ripples,\u201d which are a marker of epileptogenic tissue and can be observed in rodent models of schizophrenia and Alzheimer's Disease. Mechanisms for SPW\u2010R genesis and function are discussed in this review. \u00a9 2015 The Authors Hippocampus Published by Wiley Periodicals,
